questions.explain: Database-per-service means each service owns its data store exclusively — no other service reaches directly into it. Cross-domain data needs are satisfied through API calls or published events, never a direct cross-service database connection.
options: Shared stored procedures that join across every service's tables in one query
API calls or published events — never a direct cross-service database connection
Linked servers between service databases with four-part naming
A single sa account shared by all services so joins stay fast
questions.q: Under the database-per-service principle, how should the order service get customer data that lives in the user service's database?

questions.explain: sp_reset_connection cleans most session state between pooled checkouts, but temp tables created in a pooled session survive the checkout — a service that creates them without dropping them will eventually collide with itself.
options: Temp tables survive sp_reset_connection, so a service must drop them or it will collide with itself on the next checkout
Temp tables are automatically dropped when a connection returns to the pool
Temp tables are visible across all pooled connections, so no cleanup is needed
Pooling disables tempdb entirely and redirects temp tables to memory
questions.q: What is the chapter's gotcha about temporary tables and SqlClient connection pooling?

questions.explain: Expand/contract: first add the new column alongside the old one (expand), deploy code that writes to both and reads from the new one, then remove the old column only after the old version is fully retired (contract).
options: Renaming the column in one step during a maintenance window at midnight
Dropping the old column first so the new version cannot read stale data
Deploying the migration and the code simultaneously so versions never coexist
Adding the new column first (expand), dual-writing, then removing the old column after the old version is retired (contract)
questions.q: What is the expand/contract migration discipline, and why is it required for zero-downtime microservice deployments?

questions.explain: Developers should set the Application Name connection property to include service name and version, which shows up in sys.dm_exec_sessions.program_name. Combined with sqlcommenter trace context in SQL comments, a DBA can correlate a slow query with the exact service, version, and request path.
options: Querying sys.dm_exec_requests for blocking_session_id and guessing the service from the wait type
Reading the connection string from the plan cache, which stores the source pod IP
Setting the Application Name connection property (visible in sys.dm_exec_sessions.program_name) and embedding trace context in SQL comments
Counting connections per database in sys.dm_os_performance_counters
questions.q: In a microservices environment where twenty services share an instance, how can a DBA identify which service a slow query came from?

questions.explain: CREATE INDEX ... WITH (ONLINE = ON) builds indexes without blocking reads and writes — essential when services are always running and there is no maintenance window. Online builds still take brief locks at start and end.
options: WITH (ONLINE = ON), which builds without blocking reads and writes (with brief locks at start/end)
WITH (MAXDOP = 1), which prevents the build from using parallelism
WITH (RESUMABLE = OFF), which forces the build to finish in one attempt
WITH (FILLFACTOR = 0), which locks the table exclusively for the whole build
questions.q: Which index option does the chapter call essential for schema changes on always-running microservices?
